title: Graph state: handle changes against transported priors
lede: A node is one smile: one underlying at one expiry. The graph estimates how far today's market has moved each node's three ATM handles away from its saved prior.
eq_labels: 1 · Three handles $y_i$: level, slope and curvature at the money
2 · Lit node: today's fit minus the transported prior
3 · Every node after the solve: prior plus inferred change
eq: \widehat y_i=y_i^{0}+\widehat z_i,\qquad \widehat z_i=0\ \ \text{if no lit node is connected}
eq_note: $y_i^0$: the saved prior, moved to today's forward by the spot–vol rule; taken from this expiry of the active prior, else its nearest expiry, else today's fit, else a flat 20% smile. $z_i$: the unknown change at node $i$; $\widehat z_i$: its estimate.
paras: Why changes
the prior keeps each smile's own shape. The graph moves only what the market moved; a dark node stays at its prior until lit data reach it.
Lit and dark
a lit node's $d_i$ is observed today. A dark node's $z_i$ is inferred through the relations, and its band says how well.
alt: Graph canvas after a Layered Run: six underlyings on maturity ladders, 39 lit and 8 dark nodes, calendar and cross-asset arrows
caption: 24 September, after a Layered Run: 39 lit nodes (filled) and 8 dark (outlined) on six underlyings, SPY, NVDA, AAPL, QQQ, XOM and MSFT. Arrows are calendar and cross-asset relations; the largest shift is 122.9 bp.
example: Dark AAPL 19 Feb 2027, Layered Run. Baseline from the prior's nearest expiry, $y^0 = (25.4\%,\ -0.103,\ 0.645)$; result $\widehat y = (25.4\%,\ -0.110,\ 0.760)$, so $\widehat z = (-2.5\ \text{bp},\ -0.007,\ +0.115)$. The lit AAPL expiries moved between $+2$ and $-41$ bp.
notes: This section fills in the dark part of the universe. A node is one smile: one underlying at one expiry. The canvas is the desk staged on 24 September. Six underlyings, 47 nodes. Thirty-nine are lit, calibrated today. Eight are dark, and their real quotes are kept aside for checking.

The first line is the state. The graph does not carry a whole smile. It carries three numbers per node, the handles: the at-the-money vol, the slope of the smile at the money in log-moneyness, and its curvature there. For a fit they are read exactly from the LQD slice, with no finite differences. A skew of minus 0.1 means that one tenth of log-moneyness to the left adds about one vol point.

The handles are measured from a baseline: the node's saved prior, moved to today's forward by the spot–vol rule. If the ticker's active prior has this exact expiry, that is the baseline. If not, the prior's nearest expiry is used. Failing that, today's own fit, and as a last resort a flat 20 percent smile. The Inspector prints which one was used. It matters twice. The baseline carries all the shape the graph does not touch, and a weaker source enters the solve with less confidence.

The second line is the observation at a lit node: today's fitted handles minus the baseline, the market's move against the prior. The third line is the answer after the solve. Every node publishes its baseline plus the inferred change. Lit nodes land on their fit, or very close to it. Dark nodes get what the relations carry to them.

Why changes rather than levels? Levels and shapes differ a lot across names and maturities, and the prior already holds them. What the lit nodes say this morning is how the market moved, and that is what relations can carry. So the graph spreads the move, and each smile keeps its own shape. A node with no lit node connected to it gets a change of exactly zero. It stays at its prior, with a wide band and a flag. Nothing is invented.
Each handle is its own field. Level, skew and curvature are solved separately, with the same relations and a noise scale per handle.

The strip is a real node from that capture: AAPL, February 2027, dark. Its baseline came from the nearest expiry of the saved prior: 25.4 percent, skew minus 0.103, curvature 0.645. After the Run the level is still 25.4; it moved by minus 2.5 basis points. The skew is minus 0.110 and the curvature 0.760. The lit AAPL expiries around it moved between plus 2 and minus 41 bp, and its cross-asset neighbours barely moved. So the level change it received is small.
Transition: the question now is how a change seen at a lit node reaches a dark one. There are three operators for that. The next slide compares them.

If asked why three handles and not the whole smile: three numbers are what one day's move pins down across many names. The rest of the shape comes from the prior. Reconstruction, at the end of this section, turns the three numbers back into a full arbitrage-free smile in the node's model.

If asked what happens when the prior is old or far away: its precision drops. It halves every 30 days of age, and it falls with the transport distance, the log of today's forward over the prior's. A dark node's baseline also counts at a quarter of the lit tier, so the lit data move it more easily.
demo: Graph lens (Alt+1): Run, then click a dark node. The Inspector shows prior to posterior per handle, the Shift, the Posterior confidence ($1\sigma$) and the Prior source.

title: Three graph operators and what each assumes
lede: The operator is the rule that carries lit changes to dark nodes. Layered is the default, Precision the second choice, Smooth field the legacy option under Advanced.
eq_title: Each operator: a quadratic penalty $E(z)$ on the changes, minimised given the lit data
eq_labels: 1 · Smooth field: stay small, and close to the neighbours' weighted average
2 · Precision: one term per relation $z_i \approx \beta_{ij} z_j$, held with precision $p_{ij}$
3 · Layered, reciprocal part: lit nodes fixed at their observed changes $d_{\mathrm{lit}}$, zero gradient in the free nodes
eq_note: $z$: the changes at all nodes. $\kappa$: pull toward zero; $\eta$: reach. $K_{ij}$: trust weights, rows summing to 1; $\pi_i$: node weight, the stationary mass of $K$. $p_{ij},\ \beta_{ij}$: precision and amplitude of relation $j \to i$. $d_{\mathrm{lit}}$: the observed changes $d_i = y_i^{\mathrm{fit}} - y_i^0$ of the lit nodes (slide 37), stacked; $\widehat z_{\mathrm{free}}$: the changes solved for at the free nodes, the ones to fill; $Q_{\mathrm{free,lit}}$: the block of $Q$ linking them to the lit nodes.
paras: Probability reading
$E$ is minus twice the log-density of a Gaussian prior on $z$. Adding the lit data and minimising gives the posterior mean; the curvature of $E$ gives the bands.
Beyond line 3
Layered also carries one-way arcs with a remembered residual, four slides on.

head: Operator
Assumes
Far from the lit node
Direction · memory
rows: each relation is a stated rule: $\beta$ and $p$
full $\beta$ amplitude at Desk strength; the band widens
the same rules, plus one-way arcs where set
full $\beta$ amplitude; fresh lit nodes stay fixed
one way on directed arcs · each node's residual

example: Ladder 3M, 6M, 1Y of one ticker, only 6M lit at +1 vol point. Precision and Layered: 3M $+2.00$, 1Y $+0.50$, because $\beta = T_{\text{informer}}/T_{\text{receiver}}$, whatever the precision. Smooth field at its defaults: $+0.89$ at both ends, since its calendar edges carry $\beta = 1$.
notes: One question separates the three operators: by what rule does a change seen at a lit node reach a dark one? Each answers with a quadratic penalty on the field of changes. The solve finds the field that agrees with the lit data and pays the least penalty. In probability language the penalty is minus twice the log-density of a Gaussian prior. Minimising it with the data gives the posterior mean, and its curvature gives the bands.

The first line is the smooth field. It asks for two things. Every change should be small: that is the pull toward zero, kappa on the slide. And each node should match the weighted average of its neighbours: the reach, eta, sets how much that matters. The trust weights, K on the slide, form a table where each row sums to one, so a node shares one unit of attention among its informers. Each node is then weighed by its traffic in that table. No term says this move should be twice that one. How far a move travels, and how much of it arrives, come out of the pull, the reach and the weights together.

The second line is Precision. It has one term per relation. A relation from an informer to a receiver says the receiver's change should be beta times the informer's change, and the precision p says how firmly. Beta is the amplitude, p the confidence: two separate dials. Summed over all relations the penalty is a quadratic form with the matrix Q, and Q is sparse, since each relation touches only two nodes.

The third line is the reciprocal part of Layered. It uses the same relation terms. The fresh lit nodes are fixed at their observed changes; that is a boundary condition. Split the matrix into its free block and its lit block, and set the gradient in the free nodes to zero. The free block times the free changes equals minus the free-to-lit block times the observed lit changes. One linear solve. On top of that, Layered can carry one-way arcs with a remembered residual. That comes four slides on.

The strip runs the three operators on the smallest ladder: three months, six months and one year of one ticker, with only six months lit, at plus one vol point. Precision and Layered give plus 2.00 at three months and plus 0.50 at one year, exactly. The calendar amplitude is the ratio of maturities, and the precision moves only the bands: 2.94 points at three months, 1.57 at one year. The smooth field at its defaults gives plus 0.89 at both ends. Its calendar edges carry an amplitude of one, so it does not scale by maturity, and the pull toward zero shrinks the move a little. On a longer chain its move keeps fading.

Which one runs. Layered has been the default in the Graph lens since 7 September, chosen for its one-way and memory semantics. Precision is the next button. Smooth field is the legacy operator, kept byte-identical and reachable under Advanced. It is also what a bare API request solves, so old replays reproduce exactly.
Transition: the next slide opens one relation: what the amplitude and the precision mean, and why an arrow does not stop information flowing back.

If asked which operator is best: the recorded evidence is split. On daily leave-one-out over three historical regimes, Precision at the learned level tied the smooth field: 280.9 against 279.3 basis points of ATM error. On intraday replay of an ETF triangle, eight sessions on 27 July, the smooth field scored 168.6 bp, almost no better than the prior alone at 172.7. Precision scored 65.8 and the best Layered arm 73.7. The daily campaign gave Layered's solve an edge in stressed regimes. It was 14.7 bp better in the August 2024 spike and 9.2 better in the October 2022 bear, and 6.2 bp worse in the calm regime. The default is a choice of semantics. The benchmark pack is what adjudicates it.
If asked about the smooth field's third term: the legacy operator can add an optimal-transport term, which prices a move by the cheapest flow along the graph. It ships switched off.
demo: Graph lens top bar: the operator segment Layered | Precision; Smooth field opens from the Coupling pane's Advanced. Run each on the same lit set and compare the Diagnostics tab.

title: One relation: amplitude and confidence
lede: A relation states how much a receiver moves when its informer moves, and how firmly. The two answers are separate numbers: $\beta$ and $\sigma$.
eq_title: Relation $j \to i$: informer $j$, receiver $i$, in the receiver's units
eq_labels: 1 · The statement: amplitude $\beta$, unexplained part of size $\sigma$
2 · Default calendar amplitude: the ratio of maturities
3 · Each relation adds one rank-one term to the precision matrix
4 · What the receiver hears, if its informers were known
paras: Why the ratio
an ATM change $z$ moves total variance $\sigma_{\mathrm{ATM}}^2T$ by about $2\sigma_{\mathrm{ATM}}T\,z$. The same variance change at two maturities, with similar vols, gives $z_i = (T_j/T_i)\,z_j$.
Two dials
one known informer gives the mean $\beta_{ij}z_j$ at any $p_{ij}$; $p_{ij}$ sets only the band.

head: Symbol
Meaning
rows: ATM change at receiver $i$ and informer $j$; 0.01 is one vol point
Amplitude: receiver move per unit informer move
The part of the move the relation leaves unexplained, and its standard deviation
Years to expiry (days / 365.25); shape exponent, 1 by default
Unit vector at node $i$; the factor's direction $e_i - \beta_{ij}e_j$
The relations' precision matrix: $z^\top Q_{\mathrm{msg}}z = \sum p_{ij}(z_i-\beta_{ij}z_j)^2$
Incoming precision: $\sum_j p_{ij}$ over the informers of $i$

example: 6M lit at $+1$ point, 3M and 1Y dark. 3M: $\beta = 0.5/0.25 = 2$, so $+2.00$ with $1\sigma = 2.94$ points. 1Y is the informer of the 6M–1Y relation (the shorter expiry receives), so it is read backwards: $\beta = 1/2$, $\sigma = 3.14/2$, so $+0.50 \pm 1.57$. The two $\sigma$ are the next slide's calendar rule, $\sigma = \sqrt{(0.97 + \sqrt{\text{gap}})/1700}$: 2.94 at a 0.25-year gap, 3.14 at 0.5. Multiplying every $p$ by 100 keeps the moves and divides the bands by 10.
notes: A relation has two ends: the informer and the receiver. The first line is the whole statement. The receiver's change equals beta times the informer's change, plus a part the relation does not explain, of size sigma. Beta is the amplitude. Sigma is the confidence, and the precision p, one over sigma squared, says the same thing the other way round. Everything is in the receiver's units: vol points of its ATM level.

The second line is the default amplitude of a calendar relation: the ratio of maturities, informer over receiver, raised to a shape exponent that is one by default. Why the ratio? Total variance is vol squared times time. A small ATM change moves total variance by roughly twice the vol, times the maturity, times the change. If the same amount of total variance arrives at both maturities, and their vol levels are similar, the changes are inversely proportional to maturity. Plus one point at six months reads as plus two at three months and plus a half at one year. It is a chosen scaling, accurate for small moves and similar vols. The day-horizon data identify it only weakly, so it is kept for what it means.

The third line is the penalty of one relation: the precision times the squared miss, the receiver's change minus beta times the informer's change. As a matrix it is rank one. Its direction, u on the slide, is the unit vector at the receiver minus beta times the unit vector at the informer. It touches two nodes only, and it is never negative, whatever the sign of beta. The relations' precision matrix is the sum of these terms: sparse, and valid by construction.

The fourth line is what a receiver hears. If its informers' changes were known, its best estimate is the average of their messages, each message being beta times the informer's change, weighted by the relation precisions. The precisions add up to the incoming precision, q on the slide. Two informers with the same precision that disagree cancel out, and the receiver's precision doubles. Disagreement is information, not silence.

So amplitude and confidence do not mix. With one known informer, the receiver's mean is beta times the informer's change, whatever the precision. Halving the trust widens the band; it does not shrink the move. In a larger network the precision can change a mean indirectly, by changing how much each of several competing informers counts. That is weighting, not shrinking.

The strip is the reference ladder. Six months is lit at plus one point; three months and one year are dark, at Desk strength. Three months receives an amplitude of two: plus 2.00, with a one-sigma band of 2.94 points. That band is the relation's own sigma. The next slide's calendar rule sets it from the maturity gap: the square root of 0.97 plus the root of the gap, over 1,700. It gives 2.94 at a quarter-year gap and 3.14 at a half-year gap. One year is the informer of the six-month to one-year relation, because the automatic calendar relations always make the shorter expiry the receiver. So it is read backwards: amplitude one half, sigma halved from 3.14 to 1.57. Plus 0.50. Scale every precision up by a hundred and the moves do not change. With six months fixed, the bands shrink tenfold.
Transition: the next slide is the app's editor for exactly these numbers, the relation card, and the reverse reading just used.

If asked why the arrow does not make the relation one-way: in the Precision operator one relation is one symmetric Gaussian term. Observing the receiver rightly informs an uncertain informer. The arrow fixes the units and the bookkeeping, not causality. One-way influence is a directed arc in the Layered operator.
If asked about a negative amplitude: it is allowed, and the term stays a valid penalty. The canvas draws such an arrow in rose.
demo: Coupling pane: the live line '6M informs 3M: +1.00 pt → +2.00 pt message · relationship uncertainty 2.94 pt' follows the dials.

title: Calendar and cross-asset relation controls
lede: Two sliders set the default confidence of every automatic relation. Clicking an arrow opens the relation card, which edits that one relation: its confidence $\sigma$, its amplitude $\beta$ and, in Layered, its direction.
eq_title: How a relation's default confidence is set, and how it reads from its other end
eq_labels: 1 · Calendar relation between expiries $T_i$ and $T_j$: confidence falls slowly with the gap
2 · The same relation read from the other end: same penalty, the other node's units
eq_note: $p_0 = 1700$ per $\text{vol}^2$ and $\varepsilon_T = 0.97\ \sqrt{\text{years}}$, both fitted on stored day-over-day moves of adjacent expiries. So $\sigma = 2.55$ points at a one-week gap, $2.94$ at three months, $3.40$ at one year; the shorter expiry is the receiver. Cross-asset relations, same expiry: $\beta = 1$ and one constant $p_\times = 1.3 \times 10^4$, $\sigma = 0.88$ point.
paras: Two sliders
Calendar moves $p_0$; it reads $2.43$ points, the $\sigma$ at a reference gap where $\varepsilon_T + \sqrt{\text{gap}} = 1$. Cross-asset moves $p_\times$.
One card

confidence: AUTO from line 1, or a value; amplitude $\beta$: the maturity ratio by default; semantics (Layered): reciprocal, as every automatic relation is, or directed, a one-way arc. Its last line is line 2, the reverse reading.
Editing
every change stages a draft; Live previews it without recording; Run solves and records it; Apply activates it, Discard reverts.
alt: Relation card for a MSFT calendar relation: class calendar, confidence sigma 3.09 points on auto, beta 1.755 on all handles, semantics auto reciprocal, reverse reading beta 0.57 sigma 1.76 points
caption: 24 September, MSFT relation card: 17 Sep 2027 informs 16 Apr 2027. $\beta = 358/204 = 1.755$, the ratio of days to expiry, and $\sigma = 3.09$ points from line 1; read backwards (bottom left), $\beta = 0.57$ and $\sigma = 1.76$ points.
example: Gap 154 days $= 0.422$ years, $\sqrt{0.422} = 0.649$: $p = 1700/(0.97 + 0.649) = 1050$, $\sigma = 1/\sqrt{1050} = 3.09$ points. $+1$ point in September 2027 predicts $+1.755$ in April 2027, give or take $3.09$; read backwards, $+1$ in April predicts $+0.57$ in September, give or take $1.76$.
reference: Note 14 · Graph lens relation card, 24 September 2026
notes: This slide is the editor for the numbers on the previous one, at two levels. The Coupling pane sets the defaults for whole classes of relations, with two sliders. The relation card opens when you click an arrow, and edits one relation.

The first line is the default confidence of a calendar relation. Its precision is a base precision divided by a constant plus the square root of the maturity gap; sigma is one over the root of that. Both constants were fitted on stored day-over-day moves of adjacent expiries. The base precision is 1,700 per vol squared and the constant is 0.97. The constant dominates, so the confidence is nearly flat in the gap: 2.55 points at one week, 2.94 at three months, 3.40 at one year.

The Calendar slider moves the base precision. Its readout, 2.43 points, is the sigma at a reference gap, the gap where the constant plus the root of the gap equals one. So a single number summarises the whole curve. Cross-asset relations, between names at the same expiry, get an amplitude of one and one constant precision: 13,000 per vol squared, which is 0.88 of a point. That seed was measured on ticker medians, so it is on the confident side. The Cross-asset slider is there to loosen it.

The second line is the reverse reading. One relation is one penalty term: the precision times the squared miss of the receiver's change against beta times the informer's change. Written from the other end, the same term is the precision times beta squared, times the squared miss of the informer's change against the receiver's change over beta. So read backwards the amplitude is one over beta, and the sigma is the sigma over beta. The card prints that on its last line. It is the same relation in the other node's units, not a second relation.

The strip is the MSFT card of 24 September: September 2027 informs April 2027. The amplitude is 358 over 204 days, 1.755. The gap is 154 days, 0.422 years, with a square root of 0.649. Add 0.97 to get 1.619. Divide 1,700 by that to get 1,050. One over its root is 3.09 points, the AUTO sigma on the card. Read backwards: amplitude 0.57, sigma 1.76.

The card has three fields. Confidence is either AUTO, the first line's rule, or a value you type. Amplitude is the maturity ratio by default, editable, with a link across the three handles. Semantics, which only Layered reads, is reciprocal, as every automatic relation is, or directed, a one-way arc. The next slides explain directed arcs.

Editing follows one rule: what you see is what runs. Every slider move stages a draft. Live re-solves the draft as a preview and records nothing. Run solves it and records the result. Apply makes the draft the active configuration, with an entry in the event log. Discard reverts it.
Transition: with the relations and their confidences set, the next slide solves them all at once, and shows why a source reached by two routes must still count once.

If asked about Desk and Learned under Advanced: they set the amplitude level of the Precision solve. Desk passes the full amplitude. Learned passes the share measured on stored day-over-day moves: 0.23 for calendar relations and 0.39 for cross-asset ones. The Layered solve, as built today, always passes the full amplitude and does not read this switch.

If asked whether to add the reverse arrow: under reciprocal semantics, no. The reverse reading is already implied by the second line. The plus-reverse button adds a second, explicit relation, which only means something for a directed arc. Two directed arcs facing each other form a cycle, and the Layered solve rejects that.
demo: Graph lens: the Coupling pane's two sliders; click an arrow for its card; Advanced holds Desk | Learned, the amplitude level of the Precision solve.

title: The joint posterior and shared information
lede: All relations and all lit changes are solved together, one linear system per handle. A source reached by two routes then counts once.
eq_title: The Precision operator's solve, one handle at a time
eq_labels: 1 · Posterior precision: relations, anchors, lit observations
2 · Posterior mean and covariance
3 · A lit change is uncertain twice: today's fit and the baseline
4 · Reported $1\sigma$: the marginal; a dark node adds its baseline once
paras: Which number is the confidence

the marginal $\Sigma^+_{ii}$. The incoming $q_i$ treats the informers as exact: dark AAPL Feb 2027 on 24 September had $q = 29{,}642$, a conditional $1/\sqrt{q} = 0.58$ point, and a final $\pm 4.35$ points.
No lit path
a group of nodes with no lit node is not solved: $\widehat z = 0$, the prior, with a band of about 3 points on the level.

head: Symbol
Meaning
rows: Posterior mean of the changes, and their covariance
The relations' precision matrix, previous slides
Pull toward zero, $p_{\max}(1-\rho)/\rho$, $p_{\max}$ the node's firmest relation; 0 at Desk
Unit vector and observed change at lit node $s$
Precision of $d_s$: fit and baseline combined
$1/\mathrm{rms}^2$, cut for few quotes, wide spreads, old data
Baseline precision: source tier, cut by age and transport; $\times 0.25$ if dark
Incoming precision $\sum_j p_{ij}$: conditional, not the band

example: A lit with variance $1/p$; relations A–B, A–C, B–C, all $\beta = 1$ and precision $p$. The routes to C, direct ($1/p$) and via B ($2/p$), combine to $2/(3p)$; A's own $1/p$ enters once: $\mathrm{Var}(z_C) = 5/(3p)$. Independent routes would count A twice: $6/(5p)$, 28% too small; at $\sigma = 1$ point, 1.10 against 1.29.
notes: Each relation gave one penalty term. Now all of them go together with the data, and the solve runs once per handle. This is the Precision operator's solve. The Layered completion uses the same algebra, with its fresh lit nodes fixed.

The first line is the posterior precision. It has three parts. The relations' precision matrix from the previous slides. A diagonal pull toward zero change, which is zero at Desk strength and set by the Learned level otherwise. And for each lit node, its observation precision, added on the diagonal at that node.

The second line gives the mean and the covariance. The mean solves one linear system: the posterior precision times the estimate equals the lit changes, each weighted by its precision. The covariance is the inverse of the posterior precision. The app works group by connected group, checks each block is positive definite with a Cholesky factorisation, and inverts it. The dense algebra is sized for universes of a hundred to a thousand nodes.

The third line: a lit change is a difference of two estimates, today's fit minus the baseline. Both are uncertain, so their variances add. The fit precision is one over the fit's RMS squared, cut when there are few near-the-money quotes, wide spreads or old data. The baseline precision comes from the prior's source, its age and how far it was transported.

The fourth line is the reported one-sigma: the marginal, the diagonal of the covariance. For a lit node the baseline uncertainty is already inside its observation precision. For a dark node its own baseline variance is added here, once. Then a floor: a dark node's ATM band cannot be narrower than a set fraction of that name's recent innovations.

Why solve jointly? The strip. Node A is lit, with variance one over p. Three relations, A to B, A to C and B to C, each with precision p and amplitude one. C hears A twice: directly, and through B. The relation noise on the two routes is independent, one over p on the direct route and two over p through B. In parallel they combine to two over three p. But A's own uncertainty is common to both routes and enters once: plus one over p, so five over three p in total. Treat the two routes as independent messages, and A's uncertainty is averaged down as if there were two As: six over five p. That is 28 percent too little variance, 39 percent too much confidence.

Which number is the confidence? The incoming precision is the sum of the precisions arriving at a node: what it would know if its informers were exact. They are not. On 24 September the dark AAPL February node had an incoming precision of 29,642 per vol squared, a conditional sigma of 0.58 of a point. Its final band was plus or minus 4.35 points. The final band is the one to read. The Inspector shows both.
No lit path. A group of nodes with no lit node in it is never solved into a number. Its change stays zero, the prior, with a flag and a band of one typical move, about three points on the ATM level.

Transition: Precision treats every relation as symmetric and has no memory. The next slide adds the two things a desk often asks for: one-way influence, and a memory of each name's own dislocation. That is the Layered operator.

If asked why not pass messages node by node, as in belief propagation: on a graph with loops, local message passing can count a source more than once. That is exactly the strip's error. The joint solve is exact for any topology at this size.

If asked about correlated informers, say SPY and QQQ on one macro shock: the joint solve prices shared routes, but a common factor behind two sources is not modelled. The incoming precision adds their precisions as if they were independent. That is recorded as open work.

title: Layered propagation and residual memory
lede: Layered runs in two layers: one-way arcs first, where a target's mark is its sources' prediction plus its own remembered dislocation; then the reciprocal completion.
eq_title: Layer 1, the directed arcs; then layer 2, the reciprocal completion
eq_labels: 1 · Layer 1, directed arc $j \to i$: the sources' prediction $s_i$ plus the target's residual $u_i$
2 · The residual: set when the target prints, then halved every $H$ days
3 · Layer 2: fresh lit nodes fixed at $d_{\mathrm{lit}}$; the layer-1 marks as soft anchors
eq_note: $m_i$: mark of node $i$; $s_i$: systematic part, the precision-weighted average of the sources' messages $\beta_{ij}m_j$. $d_i$: the change the target printed; $u_i$: what it left unexplained; $\Delta$: days since it; $H$: half-life, never by default. $d_{\mathrm{lit}}$: the fresh lit nodes' changes; $V_i$: variance of a layer-1 mark.
paras: Why one-way
an index informs its names; a name printing cheap must not mark the index down. The name's own dislocation lives in its residual.
Memory in the default
each Layered Run stores every fresh lit node's change. If the node is dark at a later Run, that change anchors it, unchanged while $H$ is never.
alt: Illustrative source and target innovations over four steps: the target follows the source, prints 3 points below it, and keeps that gap when the source moves on
caption: Illustrative, $\beta = 1$, $H$ never. The target follows its source to $+13$, then prints $+10$: residual $-3$. The source moves to $+14$; the target marks $14 - 3 = +11$. The source's path never reacts to the target's print.
example: $H = 5$ days, the source moving one day after the print: $u = -3 \times 2^{-1/5} = -2.61$, so the target marks $14 - 2.61 = +11.39$; after 5 days $u = -1.50$. With $H$ never, $u$ stays at $-3$ until the next print.
notes: Precision is symmetric and has no memory: every relation works both ways, and nothing is carried from one Run to the next. Layered adds both things, in two layers.

Layer one is the directed arcs, evaluated sources first. The first line: along an arc from a source to a target, the target's mark is the sources' prediction plus the target's own residual. The prediction is the systematic part: the same precision-weighted, amplitude-scaled average of the sources' marks as on the relation slide. The residual is the part of the target's last print that the sources did not explain. The arcs must form a graph without cycles. A directed cycle blocks the Run at preflight.

The second line is the memory. When the target prints fresh data, its residual is reset to the print minus the systematic prediction. The sources are never written to. That is the cut: a single name printing cheap does not mark the index down. Between prints the residual decays: it halves every H days, H being the half-life. The half-life is never by default, so the residual is carried flat until the next print.

The plot is the smallest story, with an amplitude of one. The source moves to plus 13, and the dark target follows to plus 13. Then the target prints plus 10. Its residual becomes 10 minus 13, minus 3. The source moves on to plus 14, and the target marks 14 minus 3, plus 11. The source's path never moves on the target's print.

The third line is layer two. The reciprocal relations, calendar ladders and peers, complete every other node, exactly as on the operators slide. Fresh lit nodes, with data at most a day old, are fixed at their observed change. The layer-one marks enter as soft anchors, each with its own variance. They inform their neighbours but cannot flow back to their sources. Older lit nodes enter the same way, as soft anchors at their last change.

What runs by default matters. The automatic relations are all reciprocal, so a default Run has no directed arcs. But the memory is on. Every Layered Run stores each fresh lit node's change. If that node is dark at a later Run, the stored change becomes its anchor. At the default half-life it stays as it is until the node prints again, or until the dynamics settings are edited, which clears the store. Checked in the app: a node lit at plus one point one day and dark the next marks plus 0.99 with its memory, and plus 0.26 without.

The strip puts numbers on the half-life. With a half-life of five days, and the source moving one day after the print, the residual is minus 3 times 2 to the power minus one fifth: minus 2.61. So the target marks 11.39 instead of 11. After five days the residual is minus 1.5. The residual clock counts whole days, so two Runs on the same day see no decay.

In the app, the Inspector's Decomposition card prints the identity for every node: baseline plus systematic plus residual plus harmonic equals the mark. The Dynamics card under Fine-tune holds the fresh window, the half-life and the semantics defaults.
Transition: every operator ends with three numbers per node. The next slide turns them back into a full smile.

If asked whether Layered is the best operator: it is the default for its one-way and memory semantics, and the recorded evidence is mixed. On intraday replay of an ETF triangle over eight sessions, the best Layered arm reached 73.7 basis points of ATM error, with a half-life of a tenth of a day. Memoryless scored 80.6, never-forget 108.1, and Precision 65.8. The memory pays within the session. Carried flat, it hurt at every horizon measured.
If asked why only acyclic arcs: a directed cycle has no one-way order to evaluate. Two-way coupling belongs to the reciprocal layer, so the preflight blocks a Run that contains a directed cycle.

title: Reconstructing and displaying an inferred smile
lede: The graph returns three numbers per node: ATM level, skew and curvature. The node's own earlier shape supplies the rest, so the rebuilt curve is always a valid LQD law.
eq_title: Node $i$ after a Run; handles $y=(\sigma_0,s_0,\kappa_0)$: ATM volatility, skew, curvature
eq_labels: 1 · Target handles: the baseline plus the graph's move
2 · Retarget the base slice: solve for three moves, shape modes held
3 · Band $\hat\sigma(k)\pm1.96\,\mathrm{sd}(k)$, first order in the handle sds
eq_note: $y_i^0$: transported baseline; $\hat z_i$: the graph's move. $\theta^*$: LQD parameters of the base slice (the node's latest fit, else its transported prior). $U\delta$: three moves that change the handles, sizes $\delta$ by Newton; $V\xi^*$: all other shape modes, fixed. $\mathrm{sd}_j$: marginal posterior sd of handle $j$. $\sigma_I$: the ticker's recent unexplained ATM move. $\kappa_0$ is curvature, not the graph anchor.
paras: Always a valid law
only LQD parameters move. An SVI or MCS desk model is then fitted to this LQD target.
Never a fit
tagged graph: violet dash-dot, transported with the spot, never committed, never a prior.
alt: Archived AAPL February 2027 dark-node smile: violet graph-inferred curve, blue stale earlier fit and red current quote bars
caption: AAPL 19 February 2027, dark, 24 September. Violet dash-dot: the smile inferred by the 16:17 UTC Run. Blue: the node's earlier fit, now stale. Red: its current quotes, not used by the Run. Badge: ATM $25.4\pm4.4\%$, one sd.
example: AAPL February 2027, dark: baseline $25.4\%$, graph move $-2.5$ bp. Its ATM sd is the floor $\sqrt{0.30}\,\sigma_I=\sqrt{0.30}\times7.95=4.35$ points, from AAPL moves stored in July. 95%: $25.4\pm1.96\times4.35$, so 16.9 to 33.9%.
reference: Note 14 · reconstruction and band · graph_reconstruct.py, graph_band.py, graph/idio.py
notes: After a Run the graph holds three numbers for every node: the posterior ATM volatility, skew and curvature, each with a standard deviation. A smile needs far more than three numbers. This slide is how the app goes from three handles to a full curve, and what the band around it means.

The first line is the target. The baseline handles come from the transported prior; add the graph's posterior move. On the capture, AAPL February 2027 had a baseline ATM of 25.4 percent and a move of minus 2.5 basis points. Its skew went from minus 0.103 to minus 0.110, its curvature from 0.645 to 0.760.

The second line is the reconstruction. Take a base slice: the node's latest fit, or, if it has none, its transported prior. Its LQD parameters are the starting point. Add three primary directions, each scaled by a move to solve for, plus all the other shape modes, held fixed. The primary directions are the smallest parameter moves that change the three handles. The shape modes leave the handles unchanged to first order, and holding them fixed keeps the base slice's wings. Newton solves for the three moves until the slice's exact ATM total variance, skew and curvature hit the targets. Only parameters move, so the result is a genuine LQD law: positive density, no butterfly arbitrage, by construction.

Two edge cases. At an extreme target the Newton solve can fail. That node then shows no curve rather than a wrong one. And when the desk model is SVI or MCS, that family is fitted to the LQD curve on strikes with usable time value, so its handles can differ slightly from the targets.

The third line is the band. Each handle has a marginal posterior standard deviation. The app carries them through the reconstruction itself: bump each handle up and down, rebuild the slice, and read how the volatility at every strike moves. Square that, weight by the handle's variance, sum over the three handles. That gives a standard deviation per strike, and the band is plus or minus 1.96 of it. The three handles are treated as independent here. Their covariance is not in this band.

One more piece, the ATM floor. For any node without an observation, the ATM standard deviation may not be smaller than the square root of 0.30 times the ticker's recent unexplained ATM move. That move is an exponentially weighted RMS of the ticker's recorded innovations, shrunk toward the universe average. The floor exists because in calm markets single names move for their own reasons, which the relations cannot see.

Now the strip, because the capture looks odd at first. A move of 2.5 basis points, and a badge saying plus or minus 4.4 points. The width is the floor, not the graph. AAPL's stored innovations come from two sessions in July, between 2.6 and 9.1 vol points. They give a recent unexplained move of 7.95 points, and the root of 0.30 times 7.95 is 4.35. The 95 percent interval is 25.4 plus or minus 8.5, so 16.9 to 33.9 percent, exactly the Inspector's reading. On this capture the band tells you about that stored history, not about the relations.

Provenance. The inferred curve is stored as a fit-like record tagged graph, so it moves with the spot exactly like a fit. It is drawn violet dash-dot, with the INFERRED badge naming the Run. It is never committed, never becomes a prior and never enters a calibration. A new Run, a recalibration or a prior change rebuilds it.
Transition: how good are these inferred marks? The next slide hides nodes whose answer is known, and scores the result.

If asked why the violet curve follows the red quotes so closely: its shape comes from this node's own earlier fit, made the same afternoon before the node was darkened. Only the three handles came from the graph. A fair test needs a base shape dated before the quotes it is scored on.

If asked whether the band moves with the spot: the curve does. The band is drawn in the drill-in from the Graph lens, at the current solve. Beside it are the curve's RMS, its share inside the spread and its zeta, the standardised residual, all against the node's quotes.
demo: After a Run, a dark node's smile: the INFERRED · GRAPH badge and the violet curve. Opened from the Graph lens it adds the 95% band and RMS · in-band · $\zeta$ against the node's quotes.

title: Validation against a transported baseline
lede: Hide one lit node's calibration, infer it from everything else, and compare. The baseline to beat is the transported prior, not a flat surface.
eq_title: Lit node $i$ withheld; ATM volatility $\sigma_{0,i}$; $n$ scored nodes
eq_labels: 1 · Errors of the graph and of the baseline
2 · Standardised residual: the error in units of its stated uncertainty
3 · Coverage: share of nodes inside the 80% and 95% bands
eq_note: $\sigma^{\mathrm{fit}}_{0,i}$: calibrated ATM volatility of node $i$. $\hat\sigma^{(-i)}_{0,i}$, $V_i^{(-i)}$: posterior mean and variance there, with it withheld. $\sigma^{0}_{0,i}$: its transported prior. $r_i$: precision of its own ATM estimate. $\mathrm{RMSE}=\sqrt{\tfrac1n\sum_i e_i^2}$.
paras: What is withheld
only node $i$'s current calibration. Its prior stays, and on this desk the priors were saved the same afternoon.
Reading $\zeta$
a standard deviation near 1 means bands of the right width; below 1, too wide; above 1, too narrow. Coverage should read near 80% and 95%.
alt: Archived graph validation table: RMSE, zeta mean, zeta standard deviation and coverage for the transported prior, smooth field and messages
caption: 24 September, Validation ▸ Compare operators (LOO), 39 held-out nodes. Same day, universe and settings; only the operator differs. The transported prior carries no stated uncertainty here, so it has no $\zeta$ or coverage.
example: Smooth field: RMSE 36.7 bp, 2.0 better than the baseline's 38.7, but $\zeta$ std 0.11 and 39 of 39 inside 80%: bands about nine times too wide. Messages: 38.5 bp; $\zeta$ std 0.72; 35 of 39 inside 80%, 37 inside 95%.
reference: Note 14 · evidence and gates · graph_backtest.py, useLooComparison.ts
notes: The question is not whether the graph beats a flat surface. It is whether it adds anything beyond the transported prior, which already carries the earlier shape and the spot rule. So the comparison column is the transported prior, with no propagation at all.

The procedure. Take one lit node that has a calibration. Remove that calibration from the observations, solve the graph from everything else, and read the posterior ATM volatility at the node. Put it back and take the next one. Thirty-nine nodes: thirty-nine solves per operator. Nodes whose prior is today's own fit are left out, because that test would be circular.

The first line gives two errors per node. The graph's error is its prediction minus the calibrated ATM volatility. The baseline's error is the transported prior minus the same calibration. The RMSE is the root mean square of each over the nodes.

The second line is the standardised residual, zeta. It is the same error divided by the uncertainty the model stated: the posterior variance at the withheld node, plus the variance of the node's own calibration. An example. The node calibrates at 24.0 percent and the graph predicted 23.6. The posterior standard deviation is 30 basis points and the node's own is 10. The error is 40 bp. The combined standard deviation is the root of 900 plus 100, 31.6 bp. So zeta is 1.26.

The third line is coverage. If the bands are right, zeta behaves like a standard normal: 80 percent of nodes within 1.28, 95 percent within 1.96. The example node, at 1.26, sits just inside the 80 percent band. The screen computes both coverages from the zetas.

Now the table. The smooth field has the lowest RMSE: 36.7 basis points against 38.7 for the prior, 2 bp better, five percent. But its zeta standard deviation is 0.11. Its stated uncertainty is about nine times the errors it makes, and every node sits inside even the 80 percent band. Precision messages score 38.5 bp, close to the prior, with a zeta standard deviation of 0.72: 35 of 39 nodes inside the 80 percent band and 37 inside 95. Slightly wide, but much closer to the right width.

Why is the baseline so hard to beat here? The priors were saved earlier the same afternoon, so the prior already knows most of the answer. And 39 nodes on one day cannot separate two operators by 2 bp. Read this table as a readout, not as a ranking.

Leave-one-out removes only the current calibration. It does not make the prior independent of the target. A real test seeds the priors before the scored time, and never lets a scoring pass write stored state. The offline benchmark does that: chronological, over three historical regimes, with gates written before the run. The link beside the button opens it.
Transition: validation says how good the marks are. The next slide asks where one more quote would improve them most.

If asked which operator is better: on the recorded daily benchmark they tie. Full leave-one-out ATM RMS is 280.9 basis points for learned messages against 279.3 for the smooth field. On the intraday replay they separate: messages 65.8 bp, the smooth field 168.6, pure transport 172.7. That intraday result is why messages became the Options default on 27 July.

If asked whether a withheld node gets the band floor of the previous slide: yes. A withheld node is unobserved, so its ATM band is floored like a dark node's. On this store the floor comes from July records for SPY, AAPL and NVDA, 3.6 to 10.5 vol points, which widens those nodes' bands.
demo: Graph drawer ▸ Validation ▸ Compare operators (LOO): one solve per held-out node and operator, so start it while talking.

title: Choosing the next observation
lede: Before a quote exists, the posterior covariance says how much it would reduce uncertainty, here and at every correlated node. The plan ranks nodes by that.
eq_title: Candidate $c$, quote noise variance $1/r_c$; $\Sigma$: posterior covariance of ATM volatility
eq_labels: 1 · Covariance after the quote: a rank-one update
2 · Variance removed at each node $i$
3 · Score: the removed variance, summed with exposure weights
eq_note: $\Sigma_{\cdot c}$: column $c$ of $\Sigma$. $r_c$: precision the quote would carry, from the candidate's own chain, else the median lit node's. $w_i$: exposure weight, 1 per ticker by default. The plan shows $G(c)/\sum_i w_i\Sigma_{ii}$ in % of $\sigma^2$; the idiosyncratic floor is left out.
paras: No quote value needed
the update uses only the quote's precision. What the quote says moves the means once it arrives.
Why a node ranks high
uncertain itself and correlated with many others, like the four dark April 2027 nodes, tied by same-expiry relations.
alt: Archived observation-plan ranking: XOM, MSFT, AAPL and NVDA April 2027 and AAPL February 2027 with their variance reductions
caption: 24 September, Observation plan ▸ Rank: the five best places to quote next. The April 2027 nodes lead, three of them tied near 49.4%; XOM's incoming messages disagreed in sign. AAPL February 2027, between two lit expiries, would remove 8.1%.
example: Nodes $c$ and $j$, sd 60 and 50 bp, correlation 0.8: $\Sigma_{jc}=2400\ \mathrm{bp}^2$. Quote $c$ at sd 15 bp: denominator $3600+225=3825$. At $c$, sd 60 → 14.6 bp; at $j$, $\Delta V=2400^2/3825=1506$, sd 50 → 31.5 bp. 80% of their variance gone.
notes: Suppose you can ask a broker for one more quote. Which node should it be? The posterior answers that before the quote exists.

The first line is Gaussian conditioning on one noisy measurement. Sigma is the posterior covariance of ATM volatility across all nodes after the Run. Quoting a candidate node with a given noise variance subtracts from Sigma the outer product of the candidate's column, divided by the candidate's own variance plus the quote noise. Nothing in it depends on what the quote will say, only on how precise it will be. So the candidates can be ranked before anything is quoted. The quote's value moves the means once it arrives.

The second line reads the diagonal of that update. At any node the variance falls by the square of its covariance with the candidate, over the same denominator. At the candidate itself that is almost all of its variance when the quote is precise. At another node it depends on how correlated that node is with the candidate.

The third line is the score. It adds those drops over the universe, each with an exposure weight, one per ticker by default, so a desk can steer the ranking toward the books it holds. The screen shows the score as a share of all the ATM variance left in the universe. Minus 49.5 percent of the variance means one quote at XOM April would remove about half of it.

Two details. The assumed quote precision comes from the candidate's own chain when it has quotes: fit RMS, quote count near the money, spread. Otherwise it is the median lit node's. And the idiosyncratic band floor is left out, because quoting other nodes can never remove it.

The strip, by hand. Two dark nodes: the candidate with a standard deviation of 60 basis points, its neighbour at 50, correlation 0.8. So their covariance is 2,400 bp squared. A quote at the candidate with a standard deviation of 15 bp: the denominator is 3,600 plus 225, 3,825. At the candidate the standard deviation falls from 60 to 14.6 bp. At the neighbour the drop is 2,400 squared over 3,825, which is 1,506, so its standard deviation falls from 50 to 31.5 bp, at a node nobody quoted. Together, 80 percent of their variance is gone.

The capture. The top four are the April 2027 nodes of XOM, MSFT, AAPL and NVDA. All four are dark, no ticker has a lit April node, and the automatic cross relations tie same-expiry nodes of different names together. So each is uncertain, and each is correlated with the other three. Quoting any one informs all four, hence three nearly equal scores. AAPL February 2027 comes fifth at 8 percent. It sits between two lit AAPL expiries, so the graph already pins it well.
The tag on XOM, resolves competing signals, means its incoming messages disagree in sign, each by more than a tenth of a vol point. A quote there settles the vote.

Everything here is conditional on the model: the relations, their precisions, the assumed quote noise. A very noisy quote is worth little even at a poorly known node. And the cost of obtaining a quote is not in the score; that is the desk's call.
Transition: that closes the graph section. Next, what all of this costs in computing time.
If asked whether it re-solves the graph for each candidate: no. It is closed form on the solved covariance, one rank-one formula per candidate, no refit.
demo: Graph drawer ▸ Observation plan ▸ Re-rank: hover a row for sd before → after and the nodes it also shrinks; click to open its smile.

title: Where calibration time is spent
lede: One SPY ticker with nine expiries: the smiles take a third of a second, the local-volatility surface about three seconds. Warm-starting the surface saves optimiser evaluations: 20 instead of 66.
eq_title: Recorded 23 September · SPY, 9 expiries, 875 fit quotes · one process, quotes already prepared
eq_labels: 1 · One ticker's Calibrate job: the smiles, then the surface
2 · Local-volatility stage: fixed work plus optimiser evaluations
3 · The two recorded runs, cold and warm parameter start (seconds)
eq_note: $T_{\mathrm{LQD}}$: nine LQD-24 smile fits with the calendar screen. $T_{\mathrm{LV}}$: the local-variance surface, 253 vertices on a $368\times116$ pricing lattice. $n_{\mathrm{eval}}$: optimiser evaluations, each a forward Dupire march with its sensitivities; $t_{\mathrm{eval}}$: the cost of one. $T_{\mathrm{fix}}$: work outside the optimiser loop: seed, three post-fit reprices, response.
paras: Warm start
the previous surface seeds the fit: 20 evaluations instead of 66, same result, 3.61 bp in the fitting operator and 5.12 bp on the converged reprice.
Cached work
prepared quotes (forwards, exercise premium, inversions: 0.354 s for the ladder) are reused when only fit settings change; compiled kernels load from disk.
Parallelism
the pool fits different tickers at once. One surface is one task: pooled 2.90 s against 2.82 s serial.
alt: Bar chart of recorded preparation, LQD surface and local-volatility times on the 23 September SPY ladder
caption: Recorded 23 September after the US close: SPY Massive NBBO, mid target, i7-12700H laptop, one worker. Medians of three runs (the warm LV bar: one run). Cold: seeded from the LQD fits; warm: seeded from the previous surface.
example: Calibrate job 3.34 s, measured as one job; its two fit stages timed alone add to $0.34+2.82=3.16$ s. Before it: live fetch 1.2 to 1.4 s, quote preparation 0.35 s. One smile alone, after the fetch: about 50 ms.
notes: Every number here comes from one recorded experiment. The evening of 23 September, SPY after the US close, real NBBO from Massive. Nine expiries from two days to one year, 875 quotes fitted to mids. On this laptop, an i7-12700H, with the desk app running, one worker. The numbers describe that workload. A different chain gives different numbers.

The bars. Preparing the ladder, meaning forwards, removing the early-exercise premium and inverting quotes: 0.354 seconds. Fitting the nine LQD-24 smiles with the calendar screen: 0.338 seconds. The local-volatility surface: 2.82 seconds from a cold parameter start, 0.89 seconds from a warm one.

The first line: a Calibrate job for one ticker is the smiles, then the surface. Measured as one job it took 3.34 seconds. The two stages timed on their own add to 3.16. Separately timed medians need not add up exactly to a job measured whole.

The second line: the local-volatility stage has a fixed part and a part proportional to the number of optimiser evaluations. Each evaluation marches the forward Dupire equation over the 368 by 116 lattice, and computes its sensitivities to the 253 vertex variances.

The third line puts the recorded numbers in. About 0.3 seconds sit outside the optimiser loop in both runs: the seed, three post-fit reprices, the response. Cold: 66 evaluations at about 38 milliseconds each. Warm, seeded from the previous surface: 20 evaluations at about 30 milliseconds. Same final surface either way: 3.61 basis points in the fitting operator, 5.12 bp on the converged reprice. The warm start saves evaluations.

Three kinds of reuse save three different things. The warm start saves optimiser evaluations. The prepared-quote cache saves the exercise-premium removal and the inversions: a change of fit settings reuses them. The compiled-kernel cache saves compilation: a restarted process loads the kernels from disk.

Parallelism. The calibration pool fits different tickers at the same time. By default it has one worker per core minus one, at most eight. It does not split one surface: pooled, the SPY surface took 2.90 seconds against 2.82 serial. Starting the pool costs about 4 seconds once per session, and the app starts it while the quotes are being prepared.

Around the job. The live NBBO fetch for this ladder took 1.2 to 1.4 seconds, and reconstructing a past instant from Massive history 12.7 seconds. For a single smile the fetch is the slowest step. After it, one node takes about 50 milliseconds: the forward 4.5, the quotes 17, the LQD-24 fit 24.
Transition: speed is one property of a result. The next slide is how to read its quality before it is published.

If asked about the default order 16 rather than 24: on the same node, LQD-16 took 26 milliseconds against 24 for LQD-24, and the RMS differed by 0.04 basis points. The order is an accuracy setting, not a speed setting.

If asked whether the calendar constraint costs time: not on a consistent ladder. The solver screens first and repairs only proven violations. Here it found none: 338 milliseconds against 340 with the constraint off. When a repair does fire it costs time, and this ladder does not measure that.

title: Reading fit quality and publication state
lede: The Quality lens reads cached fits only; it never refits. A lit node is ready when every gate passes; other diagnostics are shown but do not block.
eq_title: Quotes $i$ of one node, weights $\lambda_i$, target band $[\sigma^{\mathrm{lo}}_i,\sigma^{\mathrm{hi}}_i]$ or mid $\sigma^{\mathrm{mid}}_i$
eq_labels: 1 · Error of quote $i$ against its target band: zero inside
2 · Node RMS on the fit's own weights
eq_note: $\sigma(k_i)$: displayed model at quote $i$; with a mid target, $e_i=\sigma(k_i)-\sigma^{\mathrm{mid}}_i$. $G$: the ledger of slide 23, far minus near expiry at equal rank. $g$: Durrleman's function, $g\ge0$ is a non-negative density. Calendar and butterfly failures also block an export.

head: Gate
Ready requires
QQQ 18-Dec-26
rows: fit on current inputs; data under 120 min

alt: Archived Quality lens: readiness tiles, per-ticker rollup, node table and the QQQ December 2026 node card
caption: 24 September, Quality lens: publish ready 38/39, arbitrage flags 1 (QQQ), median RMS 6.6 bp, worst 26.5 bp (NVDA November 2026), LV surfaces 4/4 arbitrage-free. Card: QQQ December 2026.
example: 38 of 39 lit nodes ready. The exception, QQQ February 2027 (RMS 2.2 bp), fails the calendar certificate against January: minimum gap $-0.1$ bp of the forward at $k=-1.70$.
notes: The Quality lens is a read-only summary: it reads the cached calibrations and never triggers a fit. It grades lit nodes. The eight dark nodes are graph targets and are not graded here.

The first line is the error of one quote, measured against the fit target. With a band target, bid–ask or haircut, it is the distance outside the band, and zero anywhere inside. With a mid target it is simply model minus mid.

The second line is the node RMS. It weights those errors with the fit's own weights, the ones the calibration summed. So it reads: how well did the fit meet its own objective. In haircut mode an RMS of 2 basis points means the curve is almost everywhere inside the tightened bands. It does not mean the curve is 2 bp from the mids. The maximum matters too. QQQ December has an RMS of 2.3 bp, and its worst quote is 16.3 bp outside its band.

The table lists the gates. A node is ready only if all of them pass. Freshness: the fit was calibrated on the current inputs, otherwise it is stale, and the chain is under 120 minutes old. QQQ's was 25 minutes: amber past 20, but not failing. Fit error: under a 50 bp budget. Wing slopes: Lee's limit of 2. Calendar: the exact minimum, over the whole line, of the far expiry's ledger minus the near one's, not below minus ten to the minus six. Butterfly: Durrleman's function, whose sign is the sign of the density, non-negative on the traded range.

Two of these also block an export: calendar and butterfly, together with any curve region below intrinsic. A publish containing such a node is refused. A draft can still be exported, stamped as a draft. Staleness, RMS and data age lower readiness but do not block the export.
Shown but not gating: arbitrage checks on the extrapolated wings, the filter's contamination flag, the count of screened quotes, the MCS calendar certificate. They inform; they do not block.

The strip. On 24 September, 38 of the 39 lit nodes were ready. The exception, QQQ February 2027, fits well at 2.2 bp. The sampled calendar screen passed. The exact certificate against January did not: a minimum gap of minus 0.1 bp of the forward, at a log-moneyness of minus 1.70, deep in the put wing. One failure, and the node is not ready.
Each export writes a manifest: the chains, the settings and the artifact, hashed and chained to the previous publish, so a published surface can be reproduced later.
Transition: next, the whole sequence on two nodes, from quotes to this screen.

If asked what stale means exactly: something the fit depends on changed after it was made: a new chain, a forward, a setting, an edit, an event or a prior. The displayed curve is then the old fit transported, not a new calibration.
demo: Quality lens (Alt+5): tiles, per-ticker rollup, node table with Exceptions first; a node card's certificates and data age.

title: A worked sequence on the 24 September desk
lede: One liquid node, QQQ December 2026, and one dark node, AAPL February 2027, followed from quotes to the publish check. Every value is read off the archived captures.

Where in the app
What to read on 24 September

$w=\sigma^2T$ for 9 expiries, chip 1 cal. cross; December against November: gap $1.7\times10^{-17}\ge0$

Production against Free; filter gains $K$ 0.61, 0.11, 0.00 for ATM, skew, curvature

notes: To finish the technical part, one pass through the whole calculation on the desk staged on 24 September. A liquid node, QQQ December 2026, and a dark one, AAPL February 2027. Every value in the table is read off the archived captures.

Step one, the market input. The Table view shows what the fit will see: the chain stamped 15:42:09 UTC, spot 736.05, the parity forward 742.89, 0.233 years to expiry, 225 strikes. Check the time stamp and the forward before anything else.

Step two, one smile. LQD of order 24 on the haircut target: ATM 20.5 percent, skew minus 0.355, curvature 4.01. The tail scales are 0.628 on the left and 0.056 on the right. The left tail is the heavy one, as expected for an index.

Step three, the ladder. Read total variance, vol squared times time, across the nine expiries, not annualised volatility. The Quality card gives the calendar certificate against November: a gap of 1.7 times ten to the minus seventeen, so the ladder is ordered.

Step four, move the spot. With the SSR rule at 1.5, the fit stays and the curve is transported. The strip: QQQ falls one percent, so the log move is minus 0.01. The ATM volatility moves by the rule's ratio times the skew times the log move: 1.5 times minus 0.355 times minus 0.01, plus 53 basis points, before any refit. Under sticky strike, with the ratio at 1, it would be plus 35.5.

Step five, earlier information. The Fit switch compares the production fit with the free one. The FILTER badge gives the Kalman gains: 0.61 on the ATM, 0.11 on the skew, zero on the curvature. The filter trusts the new ATM a lot, and the new curvature not at all.

Step six, the dark node. AAPL February 2027 has no observation. Its baseline is a nearest-expiry prior at 25.4 percent. The Run moves it by minus 2.5 bp, with one standard deviation of 435 bp, the band floor from earlier. Its smile shows the violet inferred curve.

Step seven, score and plan. Leave-one-out over 39 lit nodes: 38.7 bp for the transported prior, 36.7 for the smooth field, 38.5 for messages. The observation plan says the next quote should be XOM April 2027, which would remove about half the remaining ATM variance.
Step eight, the publish check. Thirty-eight of 39 nodes are ready. QQQ February 2027 fails the calendar certificate, and an export containing it would be refused.
Transition: that is the whole chain. One last slide to put it in one picture.

title: One calculation, read in dependency order
lede: Every number on the desk is observed, fitted, carried or inferred. Each step between them adds one assumption, and the app shows it beside the number.
paras: Observed
quotes brought to one spot and time, the forward and discount from parity, the early-exercise premium removed.
Fitted
one smile per expiry, LQD, SVI or MCS, or one local-variance surface, read with its target, weights, tails and calendar order.
Carried
a fit moved with the spot by the spot–vol rule $R$, a prior where quotes are thin, a filter across time.
Inferred
dark nodes from the graph: baseline plus a relation-weighted move, rebuilt as a smile with its band; never a fit, never a prior.
Dated
timings from the 23 September SPY run; captures and scores from the 24 September session.
reference: Questions · O opens the contents to return to any topic · the speaker notes carry equations, examples and sources per slide
notes: To close, the one idea that organised the talk. Every number on the desk is one of four kinds: observed, fitted, carried or inferred. Each step from one kind to the next adds one assumption, and the app shows that assumption next to the number it produced.

Observed. Raw quotes are not yet comparable. The app synchronises them to one spot and one time, takes the forward and the discount from put–call parity, and removes the early-exercise premium with the tree. The assumptions are the spot rule used for synchronisation, the dividend model and the tree.

Fitted. One smile per expiry, or one local-variance surface. A fit is only readable with its objective, mid, band or haircut, with its weights, its tail policy and its calendar coupling. LQD is a valid law for any parameters. The certificates check what a model does not guarantee by itself, across expiries and on the traded range.

Carried. Between calibrations the fit moves with the spot by the chosen rule. Where quotes are thin, a prior supplies what the market does not. Across time, the filter weighs a new estimate against the transported one. Each is visible: the transported curve, the prior's active rows, the filter's gain.

Inferred. For the dark nodes, the graph starts from the transported prior and adds a move carried by stated relations, with a marginal uncertainty. The result is rebuilt as a proper smile, drawn in violet, and it never comes back as a fit or a prior.

And dated. Every timing and every score belongs to the run that produced it: the 23 September SPY experiment for speed, the 24 September session for the captures, the validation table and the plan. Numbers from different runs are not added together.
Thank you. Questions are welcome, by topic. The O key opens the contents to jump to any slide. The speaker notes carry the equations and the worked examples for each one.
